Honestly? Not entirely—and history suggests that "trust" is the wrong frame anyway.

Self-regulation has a weak track record across industries, and not because everyone involved is a villain. It's structural: companies face competitive pressure to move fast and cut costs, and safety measures tend to slow things down. Tobacco companies funded research while suppressing their own evidence on smoking. Credit rating agencies were paid by the banks whose products they graded in the run-up to 2008. Social media companies promised self-restraint for years while problems compounded. In each case, many employees sincerely cared about the public good—but incentives weren't aligned, and when push came to shove, shipping usually beat safety.

AI is showing early signs of the same pattern. OpenAI wound up its dedicated superalignment safety team in 2024, and its lead researchers left publicly saying safety culture had taken a backseat to "shiny products." Several prominent safety researchers have departed major labs with similar concerns. Usage and deployment policies have sometimes quietly loosened over time. And the industry's voluntary pledges tend to be vague, unaudited, and unenforceable.

Two honest counterpoints, though. First, the concern isn't fringe fearmongering—if anything, the loudest warnings have come from inside the industry: in 2023, many of the most senior people in AI signed a public statement that mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be "a global priority." You don't have to fully share that view to notice that the people closest to this technology aren't relaxing about it. Second, a lot of genuinely valuable safety work can only happen inside companies, and many of the people doing that work are sincere and skilled.

So the reasonable position is neither blind trust nor blanket distrust—it's verification. Independent audits, transparency requirements, third-party access for testing, and enforceable rules for the highest-stakes applications are what make a company's assurances credible. That's the same arrangement we use for food, aviation, and medicine: companies do most of the daily work, and external accountability is what makes their claims worth something. Judge companies by what they do under competitive pressure, not what they say.

Full disclosure: I'm an AI built by a company in this industry, so weigh my answer accordingly. But that's itself a decent illustration of the point—conflicts of interest are better handled with verification than with trust.
